The battle of Armageddon, centred on the land of Israel around Jerusalem (Walvoord, Thomas).
The final judgment on the ungodly, while the 'city' of God's people is safe (Beale).
Final judgments on the enemies of the church at the end of the historical sequence (Barnes).
The blood rose as high as the bridles of the horses

Jewish apocalyptic used this hyperbole for eschatological slaughter: 1 Enoch 100:3 says a horse will walk up to its chest in the blood of sinners, and 4 Ezra 15:35-36 speaks of blood up to a horse's belly. Later rabbinic tradition (y. Taanit 4:8; Lamentations Rabbah 2:2) described blood reaching the horses' nostrils at Bethar in the Bar Kokhba revolt (135), a later but parallel idiom.
Josephus reports that during the sack of Jerusalem the alleys ran with blood that quenched fires (Jewish War 6.406), which preterists cite as a fulfilment.
Deliberately hyperbolic battle imagery for the totality of judgment, not a literal measurement; some futurists take it more literally.
The slaughter of the Jewish War, as described by Josephus (Chilton).
The great bloodshed of Armageddon; some futurists take it literally in places, others as hyperbole or spattering blood (Walvoord, Thomas).
A conventional apocalyptic image for complete judgment (Beale, Bauckham).
For a distance of 1,600 stadia

1,600 is 40 x 40 or 4 x 4 x 100. Four is the number of the earth (four corners, four winds, Revelation 7:1), and forty recalls periods of judgment and testing (the flood, the wilderness). Jerome noted that the length of Palestine from Tyre to the Egyptian border was about 160 Roman miles, close to 1,600 stadia.
A Greek stadion was about 185-192 metres, so 1,600 stadia is about 300 kilometres (some 184-190 miles). Distances measured in stadia were standard in Greek geography and in Josephus.

The number signals judgment that covers the whole earth (4 squared, multiplied). A match with the approximate length of the land of Israel is noted by many, and fits preterist and futurist readings that tie the judgment to the land.
The length of Palestine: the judgment covers the whole land of Israel in the Jewish War (Chilton).
A literal region, roughly the length of Israel, over which the Armageddon campaign extends (Walvoord, Thomas).
A symbolic number for universal, complete judgment over the four corners of the earth (Beale, Hendriksen).
Usually symbolic of extensive judgment on the papal or antichristian realm (Barnes).

The 144,000 are the first-century Jewish-Christian firstfruits; the three angels announce the gospel to the world before the judgment on Jerusalem; Babylon is apostate Jerusalem (or Rome for some); the harvest and winepress depict the gathering of the elect and the destruction of the Jewish nation in AD 70, whose bloodshed covered the land (1,600 stadia, the length of Palestine) (Chilton, Gentry).

Reads the harvest of 14:14-20 as the final coming of Christ in AD 70, in which the end of the age, the judgment and the resurrection were fulfilled; critics regard this as incompatible with the creedal hope of a future bodily return, while proponents argue the New Testament's time-texts demand it.

The 144,000 are the faithful church during papal supremacy; the three angels are successive movements in history: the Reformation and missionary proclamation, the Protestant identification of papal Rome as fallen Babylon, and a final warning; Seventh-day Adventists identify them with the advent message beginning in the 1840s; the harvests are the climax of history (Elliott, Barnes, Uriah Smith).

A preview of the tribulation's climax: the 144,000 Jewish believers stand with Christ on the literal Mount Zion at his return; literal angels proclaim the gospel and warn against the mark; the harvest and winepress depict the battle of Armageddon in the land of Israel (Walvoord, Thomas). They see the angel's 'eternal gospel' to every nation (14:6) as fulfilling Jesus' word that the gospel would be preached to all nations before the end (Matthew 24:14).

A pastoral counterpoint to chapter 13: the church, secure with the Lamb, must persevere because Babylon's fall and the final judgment are certain; the two harvests depict the end of history, the gathering of the saints and the judgment of the wicked (Hendriksen, Milligan).

Beale, Bauckham and Osborne read the 144,000 as the whole church depicted as a holy army, the three angels as a final call and warning, and the harvests as the last judgment, with first-century Rome as the immediate face of Babylon and the end of history as the horizon.
How does the picture of the 144,000 on Mount Zion function as a reply to the beast and its marked followers in chapter 13?
Is the grain harvest of 14:14-16 a gathering of the righteous or a judgment of the wicked? What clues in the text and in Joel 3 point each way?
Why might John announce Babylon's fall here before describing her in chapters 17-18, and how do the identifications (Rome, Jerusalem, papal Rome, a future system) change the warning?
How should the severe warning of 14:9-11 be read alongside the beatitude of 14:13 and the call to perseverance in 14:12?
What do the Old Testament harvest and winepress texts (Joel 3, Isaiah 63) contribute to understanding the scale and nature of judgment here?
The Song of Moses and the Lamb; the Bowl Angels Go Out
The seven bowls (Revelation 15-16)

John sees a third great sign in heaven: seven angels holding the seven last plagues that complete God's wrath. Before the plagues fall, the people who overcame the beast stand beside a sea of glass mixed with fire and sing a new Exodus hymn, the song of Moses and of the Lamb, which celebrates God's justice and looks for all nations to come and worship. The heavenly sanctuary, called the tabernacle of the testimony, opens. Seven angels dressed like priests come out, receive seven golden bowls of wrath from one of the living creatures, and the temple fills with smoke of God's glory so that no one can enter until the plagues are finished. The chapter is a short liturgical prelude that frames the bowl judgments as holy, covenantal and just.
The third great sign: seven angels with the last plagues
The conquerors by the sea of glass sing the song of Moses and the Lamb
The tabernacle of the testimony opens; seven priestly angels come out
A living creature hands over seven golden bowls of wrath
Smoke of glory fills the temple; no one may enter

Chapter 15 is built from the Exodus story. The seven last plagues echo the plagues on Egypt (Exodus 7-12); the victors standing by a sea echo Israel on the shore of the Red Sea (Exodus 14:30-15:1); their hymn is named after the song Moses sang there (Exodus 15) and also uses Deuteronomy 32, the second song of Moses, which speaks of God's ways as just and true. Yet the words of the hymn are drawn mostly from the Psalms and Prophets (Psalm 86:9; 98:1-2; 111:2; 145:17; Jeremiah 10:7; Malachi 1:11), which look for the nations to worship Israel's God. The scene is also a temple scene. The "tabernacle of the testimony" was the wilderness tent that housed the tablets of the covenant (Exodus 38:21; Numbers 1:50), and the cloud that fills it recalls the dedication of the tabernacle (Exodus 40:34-35) and of Solomon's temple (1 Kings 8:10-11), when the priests could not go in. The angels' linen and golden sashes are priestly dress, and the bowls (Greek phialai) are the shallow libation and incense bowls of temple service (Exodus 25:29; Numbers 7). Ezekiel 9-10, where a man in linen receives coals from a cherub to scatter over Jerusalem, is a close pattern for 15:6-7.

For readers in Asia Minor the scene stood against the setting of the imperial cult. Cities such as Ephesus, Pergamum and Smyrna sang hymns to the emperor in temple choirs (hymnodoi) and hailed him as lord and saviour; the hymn here gives the titles "Lord God Almighty" and "King of the nations" to God alone. The structural question is disputed: many read the bowls as a final, intensified retelling of the seals and trumpets (recapitulation), while others read them as the last in a sequence of events. The chapter is also linked to 14:1-5 (the 144,000 with harps) and 12:1-3 (the first two great signs).
Another great and marvellous sign in heaven

Greek semeion picks up the "great sign" of the woman (Revelation 12:1) and the "other sign" of the dragon (12:3); this is the third. "Signs and wonders" is Exodus vocabulary for the plagues on Egypt (Exodus 7:3; Deuteronomy 4:34; Psalm 78:43), and "great and marvellous" anticipates the hymn of 15:3 (Psalm 111:2; 139:14).
In Greco-Roman culture portents (signa, prodigia) in the sky were read as messages about the fate of rulers; Revelation claims the decisive signs come from the throne of God.

The word marks a major new unit. The first sign showed the people of God, the second their enemy, and the third God's answer: judgment that completes his wrath. Most interpreters see 15:1 as a heading for the whole bowl section, with 15:2-8 as its prelude.
Seven angels with the seven final plagues, completing God's wrath

The plagues on Egypt (Exodus 7-12) are the master pattern, and the number seven recalls the covenant curses of Leviticus 26, where God warns four times that he will punish Israel "seven times" for her sins (Leviticus 26:18, 21, 24, 28). "Wrath is completed" (Greek etelesthe) echoes the idea of a measure of sin filled up (Genesis 15:16; Daniel 8:23; 1 Thessalonians 2:16).

The bowls are "last" because with them God's wrath reaches its goal. Whether "last" means last in time (after the seals and trumpets) or last in John's sequence of visions (a final, most intense retelling) is one of the main structural disputes in Revelation. The bowls are total where the trumpets were partial (a third), suggesting escalation.

The seven last plagues are the covenant curses of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28 falling on apostate Jerusalem in the Jewish War (AD 66-70); "last" means the end of the old covenant order (Chilton, Gentry).
The bowls follow the trumpets in time; classic historicists (Elliott, Barnes) placed them from the French Revolution (1789) onward as judgments on papal Rome and its supporters.
The bowls are the final, rapid judgments at the very end of the future seven-year tribulation, just before Christ returns (Walvoord, Thomas). They come out of the seventh trumpet.
The bowls retell the same age-long story as the seals and trumpets, but from the angle of final, unrestricted judgment on the impenitent (Hendriksen's "progressive parallelism").
Beale reads the bowls as recapitulating the trumpets and focusing on the climax of history, while allowing that they also describe judgments through the church age.
A sea of glass mixed with fire

The sea of glass first appears before the throne in Revelation 4:6, drawing on the crystal expanse above the cherubim (Ezekiel 1:22), the waters above the firmament (Genesis 1:7; Psalm 104:3) and the bronze "sea" in Solomon's temple court (1 Kings 7:23-26). Here it is mixed with fire, and the conquerors stand by it like Israel on the shore after crossing the Red Sea (Exodus 14:30-15:1). In Jewish tradition the sea was also a symbol of chaos and evil (Psalm 74:13; Daniel 7:2-3), the place from which the beast rose (Revelation 13:1).
Glass in the first century was costly and often cloudy; a sea of perfectly clear glass suggests splendour and calm.

The sea of chaos and evil has been subdued, and the redeemed stand safely on its shore as Israel did after the Exodus. The fire probably points to the judgment that is about to fall (as it fell on Egypt), or to the fiery trial through which the saints passed. The Greek "epi" can mean "on" or "beside"; many translations prefer "beside" to fit the Red Sea picture.
Those who had conquered the beast, its image and the number of its name

"Conquering" (Greek nikao) runs through the promises to the seven churches (Revelation 2:7, 11, 17, 26; 3:5, 12, 21) and the victory of the martyrs over the dragon "by the blood of the Lamb" (12:11). Refusing the image recalls Daniel's friends, who would not bow to Nebuchadnezzar's statue (Daniel 3), and the Maccabean martyrs (2 Maccabees 7; 4 Maccabees).

In the Roman world "victory" (Nike, Victoria) belonged to the emperor and was celebrated with triumphs and coins. Christians who refused emperor worship looked defeated; John calls them the true victors.

The victors are believers who stayed faithful under pressure to worship the beast (Revelation 13:15-17), whether or not they died. Victory means faithful witness, not military force, following the pattern of the Lamb who conquered by being slain (5:5-6).
Primarily tribulation saints, many of them martyrs, who refused the future Antichrist's mark (Walvoord).
All faithful believers of every age who refuse to give their ultimate loyalty to idolatrous power.
First-century Christians who stood firm through the Neronic persecution and the Jewish War.
Harps of God

The kithara (lyre) was a temple instrument used by the Levitical musicians (1 Chronicles 25:1-6; Psalm 33:2; 150:3). The elders hold harps in Revelation 5:8 and the 144,000 sing with the sound of harps in 14:2. "Harps of God" means instruments given for God's worship (compare 1 Chronicles 16:42, "instruments for the songs of God").
The lyre was the instrument of Apollo and of civic hymn choirs, including the choirs that sang to the emperor in Asia.
The victors take up the role of the temple singers. Worship, not battle, is their response to victory, and their song interprets the judgments that follow.
The song of God's servant Moses and of the Lamb

Moses sang after the Red Sea deliverance (Exodus 15:1-18) and taught Israel a second song before his death (Deuteronomy 32), which says God's works are perfect and his ways just and true (Deuteronomy 32:4). "Servant of God" is Moses' title (Exodus 14:31; Joshua 14:7). The hymn's lines are woven from Psalm 86:9-10, 98:1-2, 111:2, 139:14, 145:17, Jeremiah 10:7 and Malachi 1:11. Later rabbinic sources say the Levites sang portions of Deuteronomy 32 at the Sabbath additional offering (Babylonian Talmud Rosh Hashanah 31a; a later tradition), and Exodus 15 became part of daily synagogue prayer.
Cities of Asia had hymn-singing guilds that praised the emperor and Roma; this hymn assigns every royal and divine title to God and the Lamb.

One song, not two: the Exodus song is now sung as the song of the Lamb, because the Lamb's death is the new Passover and new Exodus. Remarkably, the hymn does not celebrate the enemy's destruction but God's justice and the coming worship of all nations (Bauckham). It interprets the bowls before they fall: they are righteous acts that reveal God to the world.
The hymn's expectation that "all nations will come and worship" anticipates the conversion of the nations through the gospel in history (Psalm 86:9 understood as a promise for this age).
The song looks to the consummation, when the redeemed from every nation worship together; it is also sung now by faith.
Sung by tribulation martyrs; the nations' worship is fulfilled in the millennial kingdom after Christ returns (Zechariah 14:16).
O Lord God Almighty

Greek pantokrator translates the Hebrew "LORD of hosts" (YHWH Sabaoth) and "God of hosts" in the Septuagint (for example Amos 4:13; Hosea 12:5; Zechariah 1:3). It is one of Revelation's favourite names for God (1:8; 4:8; 11:17; 16:7, 14; 19:6, 15; 21:22).
Domitian is reported to have liked being called "our lord and god" (Suetonius, Domitian 13), and emperors bore the title autokrator. The title Almighty denies that any emperor rules the world.
God commands every power in heaven and on earth; the plagues that follow are under his authority, not the beast's.
Just and true are your ways, King of the nations

Jeremiah 10:7 asks who would not fear the "King of the nations"; Deuteronomy 32:4 calls God just and true. The manuscripts differ: some read "King of the ages" (compare 1 Timothy 1:17; Tobit 13:6, 10) and a few "King of the saints"; "nations" has strong support and fits the next verse.
Roman emperors presented themselves as rulers of the "inhabited world" (oikoumene) and guardians of justice (iustitia); the hymn locates true justice and universal kingship in God.
God's judgments are not arbitrary or vindictive; they are consistent with his character and his covenant. His rule extends over every people, not just Israel or the church.
All nations will come and worship before you

Psalm 86:9 is quoted almost directly; the pilgrimage of the nations to Zion is a major prophetic hope (Isaiah 2:2-4; 66:23; Zechariah 8:20-23; 14:16, at the Feast of Tabernacles). Jewish writings of the period share it (Tobit 13:11; 1 Enoch 90:30-33; Psalms of Solomon 17:31).

God's judgments are meant to reveal him so that the nations fear and glorify him. Interpreters disagree whether this means genuine conversion of the nations (Bauckham sees Revelation's hope for the nations as remarkably broad), or the final acknowledgment, willing or not, of God's rule (Philippians 2:10-11).
Points to the large-scale conversion of the nations in history before Christ returns, as the gospel triumphs.
Fulfilled in the gathering of the redeemed from every nation throughout this age and perfected at the consummation (Revelation 21:24-26).
Fulfilled in the millennial kingdom when the nations go up to Jerusalem to worship (Zechariah 14:16).
Expresses the universal goal of God's judgments in every era: to bring people to recognise him.
The temple, the tabernacle of the Testimony, opened in heaven

The "tent of the testimony" was the wilderness tabernacle, named for the tablets of the Ten Commandments in the ark (Exodus 38:21; 40:20; Numbers 1:50-53; 17:7; Acts 7:44). Moses built it after the heavenly pattern (Exodus 25:9, 40; Hebrews 8:5; Wisdom 9:8). Revelation 11:19 earlier showed the ark in the heavenly temple. In Ezekiel 10, judgment on Jerusalem proceeds from the sanctuary.
Judgment flows from God's covenant law. The "testimony" is the covenant document; the plagues are the sanctions of a covenant broken. The Exodus wilderness setting continues the new Exodus theme.
A covenant lawsuit: the law that Israel was given is now the ground of judgment on the generation that rejected the Messiah (Chilton).
The heavenly sanctuary is the literal source of the final judgments on a rebellious world at the end of the tribulation.
God's holy law stands behind all his judgments in history; nothing he does is arbitrary.
Clean, bright linen and golden sashes around their chests

Linen was priestly dress (Exodus 28:39-42), especially the plain linen of the high priest on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:4, 23). The angel in Daniel 10:5 wears linen and a gold belt, and in Ezekiel 9:2-3 a man clothed in linen goes out with the executioners to judge Jerusalem, beginning at the sanctuary. Jesus wears a golden sash in Revelation 1:13. Some manuscripts read "stone" (lithon) for "linen" (linon), perhaps recalling the jewels of Ezekiel 28:13.
Fine linen was a luxury in the Roman world; the same word recurs in Babylon's finery (18:12, 16), creating a contrast between holy and corrupt splendour.
The angels are priests of the heavenly temple. Their judgment is holy service, not mere violence. The link to Ezekiel 9 suggests judgment beginning at God's house.
The Ezekiel 9 pattern shows that the target is Jerusalem: as in 586 BC, priestly figures carry out judgment on the city and its temple.
Holy angels who will execute the final judgments on the earth; the clothing marks their purity.
One of the four living creatures gave the seven angels seven golden bowls

The phialai were the broad, shallow bowls used in the tabernacle and temple for incense and for libations or blood (Exodus 25:29; 27:3; Numbers 7:13-86; 1 Kings 7:50). In Revelation 5:8 the same golden bowls hold incense, the prayers of the saints. The cup of God's wrath is a prophetic image (Isaiah 51:17, 22; Jeremiah 25:15-29). In Ezekiel 10:6-7 a cherub hands burning coals to the man in linen to scatter over Jerusalem.
In Greek religion the phiale was the standard libation bowl, shown on vases and statues in the hands of gods and worshippers.

The bowls that once carried the prayers of the saints (5:8; 6:10; 8:3-5) now carry God's answer to those prayers. A living creature, guardian of the throne, hands them over: judgment comes from the very presence of God.
The temple filled with smoke; no one could enter

When the tabernacle was finished, the cloud covered it and Moses could not enter (Exodus 40:34-35); at Solomon's dedication the priests could not minister because of the cloud (1 Kings 8:10-11); Isaiah saw the temple filled with smoke (Isaiah 6:4). In Ezekiel 10:3-4 the cloud fills the temple court just before the glory departs from Jerusalem.

God's presence in holiness and power is so intense that none may approach. Many interpreters take it to mean that the time for intercession has passed: the judgments are fixed and will run their full course.
Recalls the departure of the glory from the earthly temple in Ezekiel 10; the old sanctuary is about to be destroyed (AD 70).
Marks a point late in the tribulation after which no intercession halts the final plagues.
There comes a point in every rebellion, and finally at the last judgment, when God's patience gives way to judgment.

The bowl angels come from the tabernacle of the covenant to execute the sevenfold covenant curses (Leviticus 26) on first-century Jerusalem. The pattern of Ezekiel 9-10, where judgment begins at the sanctuary and the glory departs, is applied to the Jewish War of AD 66-70. The song of Moses and the Lamb is sung by Christians delivered from the old order, the new Israel after a new Exodus (Chilton, Gentry).

Agrees that the bowls fell on old-covenant Israel in AD 66-70 and adds that this judgment was the consummation itself: the end of the old covenant age, the Second Coming in judgment and the full opening of the heavenly sanctuary (Hebrews 9:8). Critics note that this view denies a future bodily return and resurrection affirmed by the historic creeds; proponents reply that the creeds must yield to the time-texts of Scripture.

The bowls follow the trumpets in history. Elliott and Barnes saw the chapter as the preparation for judgments on papal Europe beginning with the French Revolution; the conquerors are the faithful witnesses who resisted the papacy (the beast) through the centuries.

The chapter introduces the final judgments of the future tribulation, which come in rapid succession just before Christ returns. The singers are tribulation believers, many martyred, who refused the Antichrist's mark. Dispensationalists see the bowls as the content of the seventh trumpet (Walvoord, Thomas).

The bowls retell the whole age from the perspective of final, unrestricted judgment. The chapter's message is that God's judgments are holy, just and covenantal, and that the faithful who refuse idolatry will stand victorious and sing (Hendriksen, Milligan).

Beale and Osborne combine readings: the vision applies to the church's conflict with Rome and every later "beast", and culminates in the final judgment. The bowls recapitulate the trumpets but go further, reaching the end.
Why does the hymn in 15:3-4 celebrate God's justice and the worship of the nations rather than the destruction of enemies? What does that suggest about the purpose of the bowls?
How does the Exodus pattern (plagues, sea, song, tabernacle) shape the way the bowl judgments should be read?
What difference does it make whether the bowls are read as following the trumpets in time or as retelling them?
The bowls that held the saints' prayers (5:8) now hold wrath. What does this suggest about prayer and justice?
The Seven Bowls of Wrath and Armageddon

A voice from the temple sends the seven angels to pour out their bowls. The first four strike the earth, sea, rivers and sun in a pattern that follows the first four trumpets and the plagues of Egypt, but now without limit: sores, the sea and rivers turned to blood, scorching heat. The angel of the waters and the altar declare these judgments just, because the oppressors shed the blood of saints and prophets. The fifth bowl darkens the beast's throne; the sixth dries up the Euphrates for the kings of the east while three froglike spirits gather the kings of the world for the battle of the great day of God at Armageddon. The seventh bowl, poured into the air, brings the cry "It is done", the greatest earthquake, the splitting of the great city, the fall of Babylon and enormous hail, yet people still curse God rather than repent.
The command from the temple
First bowl: sores on the beast's worshippers
Second bowl: the sea becomes blood
Third bowl: rivers and springs become blood; the angel of the waters and the altar affirm God's justice
Fourth bowl: the sun scorches; no repentance
Fifth bowl: darkness on the throne of the beast
Sixth bowl: the Euphrates dried; frog spirits gather the kings to Armageddon; the thief saying
Seventh bowl: "It is done"; earthquake, the great city split, Babylon judged, giant hail

The bowls are a new set of Exodus plagues. Sores (Exodus 9:8-12), water turned to blood (7:17-21), darkness (10:21-23), frogs (8:1-15), and hail with thunder (9:22-26) all come from the Egyptian plagues, and the drying of waters for a people to cross recalls the Red Sea and the Jordan. The order of the first four bowls (earth, sea, rivers, sun) matches the first four trumpets (8:7-12), but the trumpets struck a third while the bowls are total. Jewish reflection on the plagues had already drawn the lesson that God punishes people "by the very things by which they sin" (Wisdom of Solomon 11:5-16; 16-19), which explains the "blood for blood" logic of 16:6. Deuteronomy 28 threatens Israel with "the boils of Egypt" if it breaks the covenant (Deuteronomy 28:27, 60), a point preterists stress. The gathering of the nations to battle on "the great day" uses Joel 3, Zechariah 12-14 and Ezekiel 38-39.

In the Roman East, the Euphrates was the frontier with the Parthian empire, Rome's feared rival, whose mounted archers had defeated Roman armies (Carrhae, 53 BC; the surrender at Rhandeia, AD 62). After Nero's death in AD 68 rumours spread that he would return from the east at the head of Parthian armies (Tacitus, Histories 2.8; Suetonius, Nero 57; Sibylline Oracles 4.119-139 and 5.137-154). The cities of Asia had also suffered great earthquakes (twelve cities destroyed in AD 17; Laodicea in AD 60), so the final earthquake would strike a nerve. The interpretive questions are sharp: is the "great city" Jerusalem, Rome or a future capital; is Armageddon a literal valley, a symbolic name or a mountain; and do the bowls describe the end of the age or judgments within history?
Go, pour out on the earth the seven bowls of God's wrath

The prophets ask God to "pour out" his wrath on the nations (Psalm 69:24; 79:6; Jeremiah 10:25; Zephaniah 3:8) and threaten it on unfaithful Israel (Ezekiel 7:8; 14:19; 22:31). In temple ritual priests poured out the blood of sin offerings at the base of the altar (Leviticus 4:7, 18). The loud voice from the temple is probably God himself (Isaiah 66:6: "a voice from the temple, the voice of the LORD repaying his enemies").
Pouring a libation from a phiale was a standard act of Greek and Roman worship; here the libation is wrath.
Judgment is pictured as a liturgical act carried out from the sanctuary by priestly angels at God's command.
Loathsome, malignant sores on those with the mark of the beast

The sixth Egyptian plague brought festering boils on people and animals (Exodus 9:8-12). Deuteronomy 28:27, 35 threatens Israel with "the boils of Egypt" for covenant breaking; Job was struck with sores (Job 2:7).
Those marked for the beast perhaps bore a visible sign of allegiance; now they bear a visible mark of judgment. Skin diseases carried shame and exclusion in the ancient world.
The judgment fits the sin: those who took the beast's mark receive God's mark of judgment. The plague strikes only the beast's worshippers, as the Egyptian plagues spared Israel (Exodus 9:26).
The Deuteronomy 28 curse of the "boils of Egypt" falls on apostate Israel in the last years before AD 70 (Chilton).
Elliott linked it to the moral and social ulcer of atheism and revolution that broke out in papal France from 1789.
A literal, painful epidemic affecting only those who took the Antichrist's mark in the future tribulation.
The inner and outer misery that idolatry brings on those who give themselves to it.
The sea turned to blood like that of the dead

The first Egyptian plague turned the Nile to blood and killed the fish (Exodus 7:17-21). The second trumpet turned a third of the sea to blood (Revelation 8:8-9); now all the sea is struck. "Like the blood of a dead man" suggests congealed, corrupt blood.
The Mediterranean was the artery of Roman trade and grain supply (the merchants and sailors of chapter 18 depend on it), so a dead sea threatens the economy of the empire.
The source of life and wealth becomes a source of death. The universality ("every living thing") marks the bowls as final and complete compared with the trumpets.
Chilton points to Josephus' description of the naval slaughter of Jews on the Sea of Galilee near Tarichaeae in AD 67, when the water was red with blood and full of corpses (Jewish War 3.522-531).
Applied to the great naval wars of 1793-1815 that destroyed the fleets and maritime commerce of France and its allies.
A literal, global death of marine life in the future tribulation.
Represents judgments that strike the commercial and economic life of godless society.
Rivers and springs of water turned to blood
Exodus 7:19-24 (all Egypt's water turned to blood); Psalm 78:44 and 105:29 recall it. The third trumpet had made a third of the rivers bitter (Revelation 8:10-11).
Cities depended on springs and aqueducts; contaminated water meant disease and death.
Fresh water, necessary for life, becomes undrinkable. The next verses explain the logic: those who shed blood are given blood to drink.
Josephus describes the Jordan choked with corpses after the slaughter of refugees from Gadara (Jewish War 4.433-437); preterists see the land's waters defiled by the war.
